questions.q: What is the real difference between a checkbox-compliance culture and a genuinely risk-aware one, according to this lesson?
options: A risk-aware culture completes more training modules per employee
There is no real difference — both produce identical outcomes
A checkbox culture optimizes for the recorded artifact; a risk-aware culture shows up in actual behavior, like reporting a phishing click within minutes instead of staying silent
A checkbox culture only exists at organizations that have never passed an audit
questions.explain: Training completion rates and attestation records can look identical at both kinds of organizations. The real difference shows up in behavior — whether people report near-misses and mistakes honestly, not whether a module got checked off.

questions.q: Why are near-misses described as the highest-value signal a GRC program can collect?
options: Because they are required by every compliance framework
They show a control working at the exact moment of human judgment, before anything became a real incident
Because they always indicate a control has already failed
Because they are easier to fabricate than real incident data
questions.explain: A near-miss — like catching a suspicious email before clicking it — shows the control succeeding in real time, for free, before any damage occurred. That's more valuable than data collected only after something actually goes wrong.

questions.q: What does a low rate of reported near-misses actually suggest about an organization?
options: That it has an unusually mature risk-aware culture
That it has eliminated nearly all risk
Nothing can be concluded from near-miss data at all
It isn't necessarily safer — it's often a sign that people have learned not to say anything
questions.explain: A rare near-miss report isn't proof of safety. It's frequently evidence that people don't feel safe reporting, which means the organization has lost its early warning signal rather than having fewer real risks.

questions.q: What role does psychological safety play in a risk-aware culture?
options: It is the shared belief that raising a concern or admitting a mistake won't be punished — the precondition for honest near-miss reporting
It refers to the physical security of the building where GRC staff work
It is a synonym for having cyber insurance coverage
It is a formal certification employees earn after completing compliance training
questions.explain: Without psychological safety, people won't report mistakes or near-misses honestly, because they fear blame. How leadership responds to the first reported mistake sets that norm for everyone watching.

questions.q: Why can an organization be fully compliant with every framework it's subject to and still get breached?
options: Compliance measures whether required controls existed and were tested on the audit date; security is whether those controls hold up against real threats every day in between audits
Compliance frameworks never actually require any real security controls
Auditors are legally prohibited from testing security controls
Being breached automatically means the organization was never actually compliant
questions.explain: Compliant and secure are different claims. Passing an audit confirms controls existed on a given date; it says nothing about whether those same controls held up against real, evolving threats every day since.
